title: Tax on life insurance — premiums and benefits
product: Income Tax Assessment Act 1997 and ATO guidance
version: Rule guide FY2026-27 v1.0 — current at 23 Nov 2026 (ITAA 1997 compilation from 1 Oct 2026)
summary: The general tax treatment of life insurance premiums and benefits for individuals and businesses, outside and inside super. Paraplanning uses it to show the effect of ownership on tax; Claims and Client Communications use it to tell a client or family whether a benefit is taxable. General information only: Caldova doesn't give tax advice, and the client's accountant or registered tax agent confirms the treatment.
rules:
1 Income protection outside super — premiums are deductible where the cover protects the person's salary and wages; benefits that replace salary or income are assessable income, whether paid regularly or as a lump sum. Where a policy combines income protection with other cover, only the income protection part is deductible (the ATO's example splits a $250 monthly premium into $175 deductible and $75 not). Premiums paid through super aren't personally deductible. Self-employed people confirm the treatment with their accountant.
Example: Tom Bradley's income protection benefit of $5,600 a month is taxable income.
2 Life, TPD and trauma cover outside super — premiums for life, trauma or critical care cover aren't deductible for individuals, and the proceeds are generally not taxable. The capital gains tax exemptions are ITAA 1997 s118-300 for life policies (for example the original owner of the policy, other than a super trustee, or an entity that acquired the interest for no consideration) and s118-37(1)(a)(ii) for compensation for an illness or injury suffered personally by you or a relative. A terminal illness benefit, or a payment under a trauma policy triggered by death, is treated as a payment under a life policy (TD 2007/4); a trauma payment for an illness falls outside s118-300 but may be exempt under s118-37.
Example: the $1,000,000 Robert Chen received as nominated beneficiary of Mei's Corella Life policy, held outside super, is not taxable.
3 Key person cover — under the ATO's long-standing ruling IT 155 (and the Carapark Holdings case), term or accident cover taken out for a revenue purpose — to replace lost revenue or profit — generally has deductible premiums and assessable proceeds, while cover taken out for a capital purpose — such as repaying a loan or buying out an owner — has neither; premiums for combined cover are apportioned. Whether IT 155 still reflects the ATO's current view hasn't been confirmed, so Caldova always relies on the business's accountant.
Example: Northcote Custom Joinery's $400,000 key person cover on George Papadopoulos is owned by the company for a revenue purpose; Marcus Tan confirmed the treatment as the company's accountant.
4 Buy-sell cover — premiums for cover that funds the buy-out of an owner are capital and not deductible (IT 155 para 9(b)). Where each owner insures their own life to fund the buy-out, the ATO has treated the death proceeds as capital and not assessable (ATO ID 2003/1189). The capital gains tax exemption in s118-300 depends on who owns the policy — the original owner, or someone who acquired it for no consideration — so the ownership structure (self-ownership, cross-ownership, a trust or the company) matters, and transferring a policy for consideration can lose the exemption.
Example: George and Harpreet each own the buy-sell policy on their own life (self-ownership); Marcus confirmed the treatment.
5 Benefits from super — a death benefit lump sum paid to a death-benefits dependant (a spouse or former spouse, a child under 18, a person in an interdependency relationship, or another dependant) is tax-free (s302-60, s302-195). For a non-dependant, the taxable component is taxed at up to 15% (element taxed in the fund) or 30% (untaxed element), plus the 2% Medicare levy — about 17% and 32% (s302-145). TPD lump sums from super are tax-free from age 60 (s301-10); below preservation age the taxable component is taxed at up to 20% plus the Medicare levy (s301-35), with the tax-free component of a disability benefit increased by a formula (s307-145).
Example: Mei Chen's Riverbend Super death benefit, including her $180,000 default death cover, is tax-free to Robert as her spouse.
limits: Caldova doesn't give tax advice: agents state the general rules, never a client's personal tax position, and refer the client to their accountant or a registered tax agent. Treatment depends on who owns the cover and why it was taken out. IT 155's currency is unconfirmed, so key person treatment must always be confirmed by the accountant. TFNs are always masked (*** *** 123).
evidenceRequired: Policy ownership and who pays the premiums
Written record of the purpose of business cover (revenue or capital), confirmed by the accountant
Accountant's or tax agent's confirmation of the treatment for business protection
For super death benefits: evidence of the recipient's relationship or dependency
